city-park-varosliget.description: Budapest's principal city park, a rectangle of about 1,400 by 970 metres behind Heroes' Square. It staged the 1896 millennium celebrations and holds Vajdahunyad Castle, the zoo, the Széchenyi thermal bath, a lake for boating and skating, and the museums and music venue added under the Liget Budapest project.
paragraphs: City Park, or Városliget, is a rectangle of parkland in Zugló, Budapest's 14th district, measuring about 1,400 by 970 metres. Its main entrance is at Heroes' Square at the end of Andrássy Avenue, and the park is bounded by Hungária körút, Ajtósi Dürer sor, Vágány utca and Dózsa György út.

The ground was once marshy pasture known as Ökör-dűlő, the Ox Meadow; the earliest mention cited by Wikipedia is from 1241, as Ukurföld. Visit Hungary says the idea of turning the neglected woodland on the city's edge into a public park emerged in the late 18th century, that the park opened to the public in the early 19th century (some sources say 1813), and that around the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries the Rákos stream marshes were drained and an artificial lake with islands was created. By the 1880s it had become a metropolitan park with illuminated promenades and fountains.

The park was the main venue of the 1896 millennium celebrations, by which time Andrássy Avenue, the Millennium Underground and the Grand Boulevard had been built. For that exhibition Ignác Alpár designed Vajdahunyad Castle as a temporary set of 21 replicas of historic buildings. Between 1904 and 1908 it was rebuilt in brick and stone, mixing Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque elements; its main façade copies Hunyadi Castle in Vajdahunyad, now Hunedoara in Romania. The castle houses the Museum of Hungarian Agriculture, which opened its exhibition there in 1907, and in its courtyard stands Miklós Ligeti's statue of Anonymus, the unknown chronicler at the court of King Béla III.

Several institutions are older than the castle. Wikipedia dates the Budapest Zoo and Botanical Garden to 1866, the ice rink to 1870, the first performance in the circus building to 1891 and Gundel Restaurant to 1894; the Széchenyi thermal bath also stands in the park. The lake in front of the castle is a boating lake in summer, and in winter the ice rink operates on the drained lakebed.

The park has changed again in recent years. In 2019 the government began the Liget Budapest project to turn it into a cultural precinct; the House of Music Hungary, designed by Sou Fujimoto, opened in January 2022, and the Museum of Ethnography opened on 23 May 2022.
tips: Take the M1 metro to Hősök tere (Heroes' Square) or Széchenyi fürdő; both are named as access points by Budapest visitor guides.
You can walk in from Heroes' Square at the end of Andrássy Avenue.
Zoo, bath, museums and restaurants each have their own pages; check the official site of each venue for current opening times and tickets.

margaret-island-water-tower.description: A reinforced-concrete tower in the middle of Margaret Island, completed in 1911 to supply the island with water and to serve as a lookout. Designed by engineer Szilárd Zielinski with architect Rezső Vilmos Ray, it is 57 metres high and today also hosts exhibitions and festival events.
paragraphs: The Margaret Island Water Tower stands in the central part of the island, next to the open-air stage. It was completed in 1911 to secure the island's growing water supply and was designed from the start to work both as a water tower and as a lookout. The engineering was entrusted to Dr. Szilárd Zielinski, a professor at the Technical University and a European pioneer of reinforced concrete who introduced the material to Hungary; he worked with the architect and designer Rezső Vilmos Ray. The official tower site calls their collaboration a major technological innovation in modern Hungarian architecture.

The official technical data give a height of 57 metres, a water tank 13 metres in diameter with a capacity of 600 cubic metres, and main columns with a free height of 13.2 metres. A concrete staircase 24 metres high and an iron staircase 20 metres high add up to 153 steps. A Hungarian tourism page names the dome hall, with its floor 27 metres up, as the highest publicly accessible level, and a Budapest article describes an Art Nouveau spiral staircase leading to a viewing room with eight balconies and views of the city, the Danube bridges and the Buda hills.

The tower was declared a monument of townscape significance in 1977. It has been operated by the island's open-air theatre since 2011, and since 2012 it has served as a lookout tower, a visual art exhibition space and a venue for the Budapest Summer Festival. The Grand Stage and the Water Tower were rebuilt in two phases, in 2013 and 2014, with funding from the Government of Hungary and the Municipality of Budapest.

The tower makes sense against the island around it. Margaret Island is about 2.5 kilometres long and 500 metres wide and lies in the Danube between Margaret Bridge and Árpád Bridge. It takes its name from Princess Margaret, daughter of King Béla IV, who lived in the Dominican convent there in the 13th century, and Wikipedia notes that its present form came from joining three islands at the end of the 19th century. Other sights include the Centenary Memorial, the Musical Fountain, the Japanese Garden and the Palatinus bath.
tips: Check the official tower site for current opening times, tickets and any closures on performance days or holidays; access to the lookout varies.
The tower stands beside the Margaret Island open-air stage in the middle of the island, so it combines easily with a walk through the parkland.
Car access to the island has been restricted since the 1980s, so plan to arrive on foot, by bicycle or by public transport.

pal-volgyi-cave.description: A cave in the Buda hills found in 1904 and shown to visitors since 1919. Warm water rising through limestone dissolved its passages, and a guided route of about 500 metres passes dripstones, calcite crystals and sharp changes of level in a system that sources put at 12 km or more.
paragraphs: The Pál-völgyi Cave lies in the Buda hills at Szépvölgyi út 162. Its own site says it was found in 1904 and has been open to the public since 1919. The commonly told account of the discovery is that the ground collapsed under a grazing sheep in a quarry in July 1904 (some accounts say a goat), and that János Bagyura, the quarry owner's son, went in after it and found the cave; Telex says Bagyura then led the exploration.

The cave is a karst cave shaped by water from below. Telex reports that carbonic-acid-rich thermal water rising through fractured limestone dissolved the passages, and that rainwater later widened them once the cave stood further above the level of the Danube. Showcaves.com adds that the same process is linked to the thermal springs Budapest is known for. About eight of the 41 algae species found there date from the time when thermal water flooded the cave, and around 660 bats hibernate in it each winter.

Length figures depend on the source and the year. Showcaves.com gives about one kilometre in 1910, about four in 1980 and 12 mapped by 1998, while Telex says the cave and the nearby caves it was linked with after 2000, including the Mátyás-hegy and Harcsaszájú caves, form a system of 31 kilometres, which it calls Hungary's longest. Only about 500 metres are open to the public.

On the guided route you pass unique dripstones, glittering calcite crystals, narrow passages and dramatic level changes. Showcaves.com names areas such as the Theatre Hall, about 12 metres high, a Long Passage where ultraviolet light makes the calcite glow, and Fairyland, the most heavily decorated part. The cave was used as an air-raid shelter between 1939 and 1944. Telex adds that the former mine guardhouse was converted into a visitor centre in 2022.
tips: The cave's own page says to take bus 65 from Kolosy tér toward Szépvölgyi dűlő and get off at the Pál-völgyi cseppkőbarlang stop.
The route has over 400 stairs and one ladder, is not accessible for people with limited mobility, and is not suitable for children under 5 or under 115 cm tall.
The constant temperature is about 11 degrees Celsius, so bring a sweater even in summer; dogs are not allowed.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and tour languages before you go.

city-park-boating-lake.description: The lake in front of Vajdahunyad Castle in City Park, where pedal boats, rowing boats and stand-up paddleboards are rented in the warmer months. In winter the same drained lakebed becomes the City Park Ice Rink, so the setting changes completely with the season.
paragraphs: The City Park lake lies in front of Vajdahunyad Castle, and the castle forms the backdrop for boaters. Visit Hungary notes that when the Rákos stream marshes were drained around the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries, an artificial lake with islands was created.

In summer it works as a boating lake. A 2026-season announcement lists 32 pedal boats, 10 rowboats and 10 stand-up paddleboards at the lakeside, and mentions summer events such as paddleboard yoga and salsa evenings on the shore. The same announcement describes the water as a lake of 60,000 square metres, but the article does not say who operates it, so check the boating lake's own site for details.

In winter the lakebed is drained and the City Park Ice Rink takes its place. Wikipedia explains the cycle from the rink's side: in summer the rink area is flooded to form a pond used for boating. A guide to Budapest City Park similarly says that, depending on the season, visitors can skate or rent a rowing boat.
tips: Take the M1 metro to Széchenyi fürdő or Hősök tere; the lake is a short walk from either, or you can walk along Andrássy Avenue.
Confirm the operating season and what is available on the day on the boating lake's own site, since boats are seasonal.
The ice rink uses the same space in winter, so the lake looks very different from one month to the next.

city-park-ice-rink.description: A skating rink in City Park with a history going back to 1870, a neo-baroque main building and a surface of about 12,000 square metres. It has hosted European and world skating championships, and in warmer months the same space is flooded to form the boating lake.
paragraphs: The City Park rink grew out of the Skating Association of Pest, founded at the end of 1869 under Géza Kresz. According to Wikipedia the rink officially opened on 29 January 1870 in the presence of Rudolf, Crown Prince of Austria, and the first race was held on 2 February. On 6 January 1871 Jackson Haines gave a figure skating show there, and floodlights for night skating were installed in 1879.

The buildings changed as the rink grew. A wooden cottage burned down in 1874 and was replaced by a stable building designed by Ödön Lechner, and in 1893, Wikipedia says, a neo-baroque main building designed by Imre Francsek replaced it; other sources give a different year for the building, so the exact date is uncertain. Championships followed: the European Figure Skating Championships were held at the rink in 1895 and the World Figure Skating Championships in 1909, Hungary's first world event of that kind.

Artificial ice was introduced on 26 November 1926, and the season grew to 105 days. Bombing in 1944 caused serious damage, though by autumn 1945 a larger part of the rink was serviceable again. In the 1960s the skating area was enlarged and standard 400-metre speed skating tracks were added.

A renovation between 2009 and 2011 restored the main building to its 1926 state, and the rink reopened on 16 December 2011. Wikipedia gives the skating and bandy surface as 180 by 67 metres, the ice hockey rink as 60 by 30 metres and the total skating area as about 12,000 square metres. It describes the rink as the only bandy ice surface in Hungary. In summer the area is flooded to form a pond used for boating.
tips: Take the M1 metro to Széchenyi fürdő or Hősök tere; the rink is in the lakebed in front of Vajdahunyad Castle.
The rink operates on a separate seasonal calendar, so check the official site for current opening times, tickets and skate hire.
Skating can be combined with a walk to Heroes' Square and Andrássy Avenue.

millenaris-park.description: A park of nearly six hectares in Buda's 2nd district, built around the former Ganz electrical works. Preserved factory halls now serve as event spaces and the National Dance Theatre, while the newer Széllkapu Park adds walkways, solar-topped pavilions and a suspended garden with views over Margit körút.
paragraphs: Millenáris sits on the site of the Ganz electrical works in Buda's 2nd district. Ábrahám Ganz founded the Ganz foundry in Buda in 1844, and after his death András Mechwart developed the firm and set up its electricity department in 1878. The Lövőház Street building, completed in 1897, employed over 2,000 people, and a large assembly line was built in 1911 and 1912. The firm declined in the later 20th century, and from 2000 it operated as Ganz Transelektro.

The park was created from the former central factory. Demolition of two high-rise buildings began on 12 August 2000, and the park opened in 2001. Two of the old halls, the Great Hall (Building B) and Building D, were kept; together with a new entrance building and an underground car park they form one of the country's largest exhibition halls. Machinery from the old works is still on display. In 2002 the design received the Europa Nostra Award for the way it revived the historic factory halls.

Millenáris has hosted well-known exhibitions, among them Dreamers of Dreams in 2001 and 2002, House of the Future from 2005 to 2007 and the Palace of Wonders series, which ran on the site from 2005 to 2012. The former factory assembly hall, Building E, is now the National Dance Theatre, designed by ZDA - Zoboki Építésziroda, with two theatre halls, a chamber hall and rehearsal rooms.

Széllkapu Park is the newer part. Its walkways lead to three mushroom-shaped buildings topped with solar panels that generate energy and provide shade, and a suspended garden, reached by a panoramic lift, looks over Margit körút, the Castle District and the Buda hills. The official site describes the area as barrier-free; pets are not allowed except certified assistance animals. The address is Kis Rókus utca 16-20.
tips: Millenáris is on Kis Rókus utca, close to Margit körút, so it combines easily with the Buda side of the Danube.
Check the official Millenáris site for current opening times, events and tickets, because hours differ between the park areas and the venues.
Pets are not allowed except certified assistance animals, according to the official site.

kopaszi-gat.description: A long Danube embankment in south Buda, created as a regulation dam between 1870 and 1876 to reduce ice floods. After decades of industry and landfill it was redeveloped from 2006 as a landscaped park with cafés, a playground and views across Lágymányos Bay towards the BudaPart quarter.
paragraphs: Kopaszi-gát takes its name from the Kopaszi sandbank that once lay in this stretch of the Danube; the name can be translated as the bare bank. Ice floes jammed against sandbars here in the 18th and 19th centuries and caused icy floods. After the Pest flood of 1838, a law in 1870 ordered river regulation and a parallel dam, and the long, sandy dam was completed in 1876. Because its southern end did not reach the bank, Lágymányos Bay formed.

The water behind the dam later divided into a bay and Lágymányos Lake. In May 1896 the Orfeum owner Károly Somossy opened Konstantinápoly Budapesten, a Turkish-style entertainment quarter, here; it lost its appeal quickly because of mosquitoes and closed about six months later. In the early 20th century parts of the lake were filled in while the Budapest University of Technology was built, and the rest was used for fish farming, boating and swimming; Alfréd Hajós often trained there. After the Second World War about 1.5 million cubic metres of soil and rubble filled nearly the whole lakebed and factories took over.

After industry closed following the political change, the area deteriorated until around 2000. From 2006 restaurants, bistros and cafés opened, a playground was built and the dam was redeveloped as a green leisure park; one visitor guide says that by 2007 the embankment had become a landscaped public park, with architecture using concrete, metal, wood and glass.

The surroundings keep changing. In 2015 the district sold the bay's embankment and undeveloped land, 57 hectares in all, and the area, now called BudaPart, was planned by the firm ADEPT, which won the 2016 planning competition. The MOL Campus tower, designed by Foster + Partners, is 143 metres tall and employees moved in during December 2022, giving south Buda a new point of orientation.
tips: One visitor guide suggests tram 1 to Rákóczi Bridge, then about a 10-minute walk to the entrance; check current routes before you travel.
The Budapest University of Technology and Economics and Rákóczi Bridge are close by, so the park fits a walk along the Danube in south Buda.
Restaurants and cafés have their own times, so check them individually before planning a meal.

zugliget-chairlift.description: Hungary's first passenger ropeway, opened on 20 August 1970, carrying double chairs for 1,040 metres from Zugliget up János Hill, a rise of 262 metres. Its nickname Libegő, meaning floater, won a public naming contest, and the top station is a short walk from the Erzsébet lookout.
paragraphs: The Zugliget Chairlift, known as the Libegő, runs from Zugliget in Budapest's 12th district up János Hill, the highest peak in Budapest. BKK describes it as Hungary's first passenger ropeway and gives its opening as 20 August 1970. The track is 1,040 metres long with a height difference of 262 metres between the stations, and the ride takes 12 to 15 minutes depending on the source. BKK counts 102 double chairs.

The idea is older than the line. In 1933 the engineer István Hantos Jr. proposed a suspension railway from Zugliget to János Hill, but only preparatory work was done, and the plans were revived in the early 1940s before the Second World War halted construction. The 12th District Council decided to build the line in 1967, construction started on 24 March 1969, and it opened in 1970. The official name was Jánoshegyi Légpálya, János Hill Air Lane, but a public naming contest produced the nickname Libegő, which means floater.

At the top, the Erzsébet lookout tower is a few minutes' walk away; Visit Hungary calls it the highest spot in Budapest, and the surrounding hill is covered with forests, gardens and hiking trails. BKK notes that the upper station has a wheelchair-accessible lookout on the terrace of a former restaurant.

The chairlift also links with other Buda hills attractions. BKK says the upper station can be reached on foot from the János-hegy or Virágvölgy stops of the Children's Railway, and by bus 21 or 211 from Széll Kálmán tér to Normafa followed by a walk of 20 to 30 minutes.
tips: BKK gives the lower station as Zugligeti út 97, at the terminus of bus 291, which runs from Nyugati pályaudvar.
Passengers with severely limited mobility are not permitted to ride, and children under 10 may ride only with an accompanying adult.
Service can be suspended in severe storms and for maintenance on set dates, so check the BKK page for the current operating service and closure days before you go.
The Erzsébet lookout tower and the Children's Railway stops at János-hegy and Virágvölgy are nearby.

childrens-railway.description: A 760 mm narrow-gauge line of about 11 km through the Buda hills between Széchenyi-hegy and Hűvösvölgy, opened in stages from 1948 to 1950. Children aged roughly 10 to 14 perform most station and train duties under adult supervision, a practice recognised by Guinness World Records in 2015.
paragraphs: The Children's Railway, in Hungarian Gyermekvasút, runs through the Buda hills between Széchenyi-hegy and Hűvösvölgy. Wikipedia gives the length as 11.2 km (its history text says 11.7 km), the gauge as 760 mm, the maximum speed as 20 km/h and the journey time as about 40 to 45 minutes. The two termini are about 235 metres apart in elevation. It is single-track and not electrified.

Children aged 10 to 14 operate all posts except the train driver, under adult supervision. We Love Budapest describes the roles as ticket inspectors, brakemen, cashiers, announcers and platform attendants. In 2015 Guinness World Records recognised it as the longest railway on which commercial traffic services are run by children.

The railway was started in 1948. MÁV decided in 1947 to build a children's railway, and Wikipedia says construction began on 11 April 1948 and the first section, from Széchenyi-hegy to Előre, now Virágvölgy, opened on 31 July 1948. The line reached Szépjuhászné about a year later and Hűvösvölgy on 20 August 1950. It was originally called the Pioneer Railway, Úttörővasút, and it closed during the 1956 revolution without damage and reopened on 3 February 1957.

The stops make a useful route through the hills. Counting the termini, the line stops at Hűvösvölgy, Hárs-hegy, Szépjuhászné, János-hegy, Virágvölgy, Csillebérc, Normafa and Széchenyi-hegy. A 198-metre tunnel lies just before Hárs-hegy. The station building at Hűvösvölgy houses a Children's Railway Museum, and at Széchenyi-hegy you can change to the Cogwheel Railway. Several stops are near other Buda hills sights, including the chairlift at János-hegy and the Normafa meadow.
tips: Timetables and tickets are on the official site, gyermekvasut.hu, which We Love Budapest says has English pages; check it for current opening times and the season.
At Széchenyi-hegy you can transfer to the Cogwheel Railway, and the Zugliget chairlift is near the János-hegy and Virágvölgy stops.
Vadaspark is a timetabled stop for the Wildlife Park, but We Love Budapest says it is served only for groups that request it in advance.

normafa.description: A meadow and plateau in the Buda hills, named after a beech tree struck by lightning in 1927, with a view over the city. It has been used for walking and winter sport for well over a century, and a phased renovation since the mid-2010s has added paths, a playground and visitor facilities.
paragraphs: Normafa is a recreation area in the Buda hills, in Svábhegy in Budapest's 12th district, and Wikipedia gives its summit as 477 metres. A long, narrow plateau connects Svábhegy and János Hill. The site is known for panoramic views, and the open meadow looks out over the capital.

The name comes from a beech tree. Older Swabian residents called it Viharbükk, the storm beech, and according to legend it sprouted when King Matthias was born, and some believe the king napped in its shade. The hegyvidek.hu page says that in 1840 the actress Róza Schodelné Klein sang an aria from Bellini's Norma under the tree because its appearance recalled a scene from the opera, and the name then spread to the meadow. Lightning felled the tree in 1927, and a plaque commemorating it was put up in 1967.

Svábhegy has attracted hikers since the 17th century. The cogwheel railway opened in 1871 and was extended to Széchenyi-hegy in 1890. Skiing is recorded from 1895, a toboggan run was built before the First World War, and two ski jumps, one small and one large, were built in the 1920s; both are now gone. The first electric ski lift opened on Kis-Normafa in 1971 and has also been demolished.

A multi-year improvement project began to renew the area. By November 2015 its first phase had repaved the main path to János Hill, added benches and rubbish bins and upgraded the playground on Anna Meadow. A February 2020 article described a further redevelopment with a new car park and visitor centre, and reported that kiosks selling strudel and snacks were set to move. Plans may have progressed since then, so treat current facilities as something to check locally.
tips: We Love Budapest says bus 21 from Széll Kálmán tér goes to the Normafa stop; BKK also names bus 21 or 211 for the walk to the Zugliget chairlift's upper station.
The Children's Railway has a Normafa stop, and the Zugliget chairlift's upper station is a 20 to 30 minute walk away through the forest.
The area is used for walking, running, cycling, sledging in winter and cross-country skiing; check the district's site for current conditions and facilities.

the-taban.description: A green slope between Buda Castle, Gellért Hill and Naphegy, on the site of the old Tabán quarter of winding streets, taverns and Serbian, Greek and German residents. The district was largely demolished in the 1930s, and today a quiet park near Döbrentei Square marks its place.
paragraphs: The Tabán is a park in Buda's 1st district between Buda Castle, Gellért Hill and Naphegy, near Döbrentei Square. The Visit Buda Castle page calls it a quiet place for a walk, a picnic or a pause while sightseeing, and says it occupies the site of a quarter of winding streets, restaurants and wine taverns that many called the Montmartre of Budapest.

The area has long been settled thanks to its sheltered valley, the thermal waters at the foot of Gellért Hill and a ford across the Danube. After the 1686 liberation of Buda, refugees arrived from Greece, Bosnia and Serbia, and Wikipedia says that in the 18th century the residents included Serbs, Greeks, Vlachs, Germans, Croats, Slovaks and Romani people. The Serbs were called Rácok, which gave the district the name Rácváros.

In the early 20th century its houses were considered unhealthy, and the Tabán was demolished in the 1930s because of overcrowding and poor public health. The area had been planned as a spa quarter, but a temporary park was created instead. Wikipedia also records the 1956 memorial near Naphegy and Kereszt streets and the Semmelweis Museum of Medical History near Apród Street. The Rác Thermal Bath near Döbrentei Square was listed as closed on the Visit Buda Castle page, so check its current status.
tips: The park is near Döbrentei Square, at the foot of the Tabán, and lies between Buda Castle and Gellért Hill, so it suits a walk between the two.
The Rác Thermal Bath is nearby but was listed as closed on the Visit Buda Castle page; check the official sites for current opening times.
The Semmelweis Museum of Medical History is near Apród Street, and the 1956 memorial is near Naphegy and Kereszt streets.
